cells.tense: You're the one deciding what gets another round — the next pass, the small correction, the part that still isn't right.
cells.ask: Show one half-finished piece of the work to someone today — the version that isn't clean yet — and later, write down in one line what you noticed while they looked at it.
cells.core:
The repetitions go in because you want them in. You're not waiting on a mood or a deadline, and you're not proving anything to anyone. On the flat days the practice still holds, and that's because you're the one choosing it, run at your own pace, watched by no one in particular. What gets built here gets built by that steady picking, not by any single good session.

There's one step further out available. Hand someone the unfinished version before it's tidy, then write one line about what you saw while they held it. What it gives you is a look at your own eye from a different angle — plain, and only yours.

cells.tense: You've already run the next several rounds in your head, picturing the version where it's finally right, while your hands are still on the first.
cells.ask: Do one round badly on purpose today — no notes, no replay afterward — and see whether it hands you back a feel for the material itself.
cells.core:
Nothing looks wrong from outside. The rounds get done, the corrections get made, and on a good day the work even feels sharp. But lately it's being measured against a picture of how it should come out, and that picture lives a few steps ahead of where your hands are. A practice meant to be lived starts getting graded instead — tiring in a way that can pass for dedication.

One round today, done badly on purpose, with nothing to review after. The point isn't the bad work; it's that your attention comes back to the actual thing under your hands instead of the version that hasn't happened and doesn't need to.

cells.tense: The rounds still get done — you're still there — but nothing in them is picking what comes next.
cells.ask: Today, pick one small thing to do all the way through, once, and let that pick be the whole point of it.
cells.core:
A practice like this has an aim: you know what you're building toward, and the repetitions serve it. That direction is what keeps the repetition alive rather than just repeated — you can feel it on the days the work has pull. Lately the movements still happen, but nothing in them is choosing the next one, so the same thing gets done because stopping would mean noticing that the aim went out.

Pick one small thing today and do it all the way through, once. Same thing as yesterday is fine. The size doesn't matter — that you picked it, instead of it running on its own, is what puts the direction back under your own hand.

cells.tense: You're the one noticing things — the eye is doing that — and your account of it says the practice is what sees.
cells.ask: Say "I saw that" out loud, once, about one thing you noticed today — something you'd normally file under what the practice produced.
cells.core:
When this is healthy, you know your own looking is doing real work. The repetitions sharpen it, but the repetitions aren't the ones seeing. You notice something new in the material, something the practice didn't put there, and you have the plain sense that you caught it. What's here instead is the credit on loan: what your eye catches gets filed under the method, the routine, the training — as if seeing were just a side effect of the practice rather than the thing the practice was built to hold.

One sentence, said out loud, once. A small thing you caught counts. Your eye doesn't change when you say it; what changes is who's on record as having used it.
